why_tested: A per-pound federal payment was the sector's primary revenue instrument
cost_or_effort: Bid preparation plus a 500,000 performance bond under Sections 426-427 of Title 39
result: WON against three named rivals at 1.50 per pound versus 2.24 - 33.0 percent below the next bid (DERIVED)
repeatability: REPEATED on other routes: the 1934 record schedules Boeing Air Transport on A.M. 5 and A.M. 18, and by 1930 the A.M. 18 contract had been converted into a ten-year ROUTE CERTIFICATE
notes: P1CHN01. The one channel this corpus can quantify from third-party paper. Note the 1934 annulment order attacking exactly this channel.

channel: Sub-contracting the flying to a separate carrier
why_tested: The bidder was a manufacturer; service had to be performed
result: The contract was duly sublet to Boeing Air Transport, Inc., a second Washington corporation
repeatability: UNKNOWN whether later contracts used the same device
notes: P1CHN02. A named-legal-person split between the right to be paid and the act of delivery.

notes: P1CHN03. Note the lease defines its counterparty as 'Boeing Company' - a contract shorthand, not a corporate naming (U.016).

channel: Equity markets as a funding channel
why_tested: Bank credit was available but expensive and encumbering
cost_or_effort: Issue expense 375,388.75 on 5,767,936 gross (6.5 percent, DERIVED)
result: 1937: 5.5 percent of the issue left with underwriters; 1940: 24.5 percent - and the 1940 money retired the secured loan entirely, unencumbering the plants
repeatability: Yes, twice inside the window, with the underwriter-take share quadrupling
notes: P1CHN07. Repeatability is real; the deteriorating take-up ratio is the negative signal inside a success.
